newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Manila prices,exports point to steady growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Manila prices,exports point to steady growth.

text.p: The Philippines should see steady growth this year after inflation fell to a ten-year low and exports surged 23 percent in the first four months, economists said on Thursday.
But, problems in manufacturing and the unpredictability of agricultural output mean that the government is unlikely to meet an ambitious target for 1997 growth of seven to eight percent.
Earlier, the National Statistics Office reported year-on-year inflation slowed to 4.2 percent in May compared with 4.6 percent in April, and the lowest since July 1997.
It also announced that exports in the first four months jumped 23 percent to $7.59 billion and for April alone they soared 39.6 percent to $2.08 billion from the year-ago's $1.49 billion.
"I think the economy is on track for steady growth this year," said Hong Kong-based BZW Asia Ltd economist Kate O' Donaghue said.
She projected a full-year gross national product growth of 6.8 percent in 1997 compared with 6.9 percent in 1996. Her forecast, however, remains below the government's bullish GNP target.

Peregrine Securities economist Luz Lorenzo, who projected GNP at 7.6 percent this year, said the latest figures show the Philippine economy has more room to grow after reporting last week a slow first quarter GNP growth of 6.1 percent compared with 6.9 percent a year earlier.
"It (inflation) would be better for growth. It means we could grow some more. No overheating," she said, adding that low inflation justifies low interest rates.
The Central Bank said it now expects inflation to stay below six percent.
In line with low inflation, the Bank earlier slashed its overnight borrowing rate by two percentage points to 14 percent.
Before the inflation figure was announced, Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters "evidence points to a cut in rates."
Far East Bank economist Emma Pante said she had adjusted her 1997 inflation forecast to 5.5 percent from an earlier 6.5 percent.

On the strong export figure, "we may be able to earn enough (this year) from our own current foreign transactions to finance the current account...instead of relying on the very volatile portfolios," Pante added.

More important than the latest economic figures, BZW's O'Donaghue said the government must pass into law this year the last component of its tax reform package, which would expand the number of people paying income taxes and restructure corporate income taxes.
"It's a necessary measure in the long-run...The tax reform is very important for giving the government a sound financial footing," said O' Donaghue.
